title: Forgiving in traffic
hook: Marcus Aurelius starts his morning expecting rude people, and calls them kin
tomorrow: why did a cook who hated the kitchen call it his best place to pray?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rose-apple shade: the queue, a wait you can breathe in. Today the wait has a steering wheel, and someone just cut in front of you.

A car slides across two lanes with no signal, and you're the one slamming the brakes. A heart can be pounding before anyone's decided anything. The emperor whose notebook opened with thank-yous, Marcus Aurelius, has another entry for exactly that kind of morning. It begins like a man bracing for traffic: "Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial."
screen: `NO SIGNAL. BRAKES.` → `MARCUS, ANOTHER MORNING.` → `I SHALL MEET THE BUSY-BODY.`

segments.voice: It sounds grim. Read on, and it turns. Why are people like that? Marcus answers: they act out of ignorance of what is good and evil. They don't see what he sees. Then he goes further. The one who wrongs him is his kin, not by blood, but because every person shares the same reason, a portion of the divine. So he can't be harmed by them, and he can't hate them. "For we are made for co-operation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth." That's the Stoic teaching, and it's specific: those who do wrong do it from not knowing the good, and every human being belongs to one shared order with you. So forgiving the driver isn't pretending they were right. The wrong is still a wrong. It's remembering two things, fast: they don't see what you see, and they're part of the same body you are. Upper teeth don't take revenge on the lower ones. In plain words, at a red light: they're having a day, and they're still kin.
screen: `THEY ACT FROM NOT KNOWING.` · `THE ONE WHO WRONGS ME IS KIN.` · `LIKE UPPER AND LOWER TEETH.` · `THE WRONG STAYS A WRONG.` · then, large: `THEY'RE HAVING A DAY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one driver, or anyone, who cut in front of you lately. Breathe in and say quietly, they don't see what I see. Breathe out and say, and they're still my kin, and let them drive on.
Forgiving in traffic: the Stoic move at the wheel. They act from not knowing, and they're still kin, like upper and lower teeth.
Take this with you: they're having a day. Marcus would add, and they're still my kin. Three of fourteen.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius rehearse Meditations 2.1 in the morning, expecting difficult people and reminding themselves that those people act from not knowing and are still kin.

fork.setup: a coworker takes credit for your idea in the morning meeting, and you're furious. what's the Marcus Aurelius move?

fork.reveal: Marcus expects wrongdoers and still calls them kin, made to work together like teeth. the wrong can be named; the hatred isn't needed.
